title: Elizabeth Loftus ·《你的记忆有多可靠？》— 记忆像维基百科，谁都能改
title_en: Elizabeth Loftus · "How reliable is your memory?" — Memory is a Wikipedia page anyone can edit

questions.question: Loftus 用「记忆像维基百科」概括的那个机制，至今被认为站得最稳。它具体是什么？
options: 事后接收的信息会混进原始记忆，整合之后人就分不清某个细节从哪来
在高压下形成的记忆格外深刻准确，比平静状态下形成的记忆要可靠得多
创伤记忆会被整段压抑多年，之后再通过心理治疗被完整而准确地找回来
记忆像录像一样会随时间褪色，越久远的事件丢失的细节越多
questions.explanation: 误导信息效应：事后信息混入原始记忆，之后只剩一个「记忆」，来源查不回来。Loftus 研究的恰恰不是遗忘；美军模拟审讯研究说明高压下记忆照样能被改写；「压抑后找回」正是记忆战争中她所质疑的一方。
questions.question_en: Loftus summed up a mechanism as 'memory is like a Wikipedia page', and it is still considered the most solid part of her work. What exactly is it?
options_en: Information received after an event blends into the original memory, and once integrated, people can't tell where a given detail came from
Memories formed under high stress are especially vivid and accurate, more reliable than calm ones
Traumatic memories can be repressed whole for years and then fully recovered through therapy
Memory fades over time like a recording, so older events lose more detail
questions.explanation_en: The misinformation effect: post-event information merges into the original memory, leaving a single 'memory' whose sources can't be traced. Loftus studies not forgetting but its opposite; the military interrogation study shows memories formed under stress can still be rewritten; and 'repressed then recovered' is the side she challenged in the memory wars.

questions.question: 按 2017 年 Wixted 与 Wells 关于目击信心的综述，Steve Titus 案中最该被陪审团听见的是什么？
options: 受害者情绪激动、细节丰富的庭上证词，说明她的记忆真实可靠、值得采信
两次说法都不重要，因为目击者的信心在任何条件下都说明不了真假
受害者在庭上说的「我绝对确定就是他」——高信心的指认通常都相当准确
受害者第一次看照片列队时说的「这张最像」——低信心的初次指认是危险信号
questions.explanation: 在规范条件下（第一次、未受污染、列队公平、当场记录信心），初次指认的信心很有信息量：高信心的初次指认相当准确，低信心的容易出错；条件一旦不干净，后来的高信心也靠不住。这收窄了「信心说明不了什么」的说法，同时说明 Titus 案的红灯在第一句。
questions.question_en: According to Wixted and Wells's 2017 review of eyewitness confidence, what should the jury in the Steve Titus case most have heard?
options_en: The victim's emotional, detailed testimony, showing the memory was genuine and reliable
Neither statement matters, since eyewitness confidence says nothing about accuracy under any conditions
The victim's courtroom statement, 'I'm absolutely positive that's the man' — high-confidence identifications are usually accurate
The victim's words at the first photo lineup, 'That one's the closest' — a low-confidence initial identification is a red flag
questions.explanation_en: Under clean conditions — first, uncontaminated identification, fair lineup, no administrator influence, confidence recorded on the spot — initial confidence is informative: high-confidence first IDs are fairly accurate and low-confidence ones error-prone, while later confidence under contaminated conditions can't be trusted. This narrows 'confidence means nothing' and shows the red flag in Titus's case was the first statement.

questions.question: 2023 年「商场走失」复制研究按编码得出 35% 的假记忆率，被试自认记得的只有 14%，另一项重读访谈稿的分析推算约 4%。这组分歧说明了什么？
options: 事后信息能扭曲记忆已无争议；争的是整段假记忆多常见、多完整，及「记得」怎么定义
复制研究证实约四分之一的比例可以推广到一般人群，争议已经平息
只要被试本人说不记得，就说明暗示性的问话对他们的记忆根本没有产生任何影响
复制研究失败了，假记忆植入已被证伪，原实验的结论应当撤回
questions.explanation: 复制研究的编码结果比原版还高，但被试本人的判断和逐字重读都给出低得多的数字。双方都承认假记忆会发生，争的是频率与完整度；原作者当年就说比例不能推广，研究只是「存在性证明」。
questions.question_en: A 2023 replication of 'lost in the mall' coded 35% of participants as having false memories, yet only 14% said they remembered, and a reanalysis of the transcripts put it near 4%. What does this disagreement show?
options_en: That post-event information can distort memory is no longer disputed; the fight is over how common and complete whole false memories are, and researchers and participants define 'remembering' very differently
The replication confirmed that roughly a quarter generalizes to the population, so the dispute is settled
If participants say they don't remember, suggestive questioning had no effect on their memory at all
The replication failed, false memory implantation has been disproven, and the original conclusion should be retracted
questions.explanation_en: The replication's coded rate exceeded the original, but participants' own judgements and the transcript reread give far lower figures. Both sides agree false memories happen; they dispute frequency and completeness. The original authors themselves said the rate couldn't be generalized and the study was an existence proof.
